title: Preserved original string for Version
body:
Currently, the `project.name` field is stored exactly as it was written in most backends, which allows the PyPI display to match the user's preference:

* [Cython](https://pypi.org/project/Cython): they stylize it with a capital C. Also SQLAlchemy, PyQt5, GitPython, ...
* [pyproject-fmt](https://pypi.org/project/pyproject-fmt): you stylize this projects with a `-`
* [jaraco.packaging](https://pypi.org/project/jaraco.packaging): all of jaraco's packages use dots. It's also common for namespace packages (zope, backports, etc).
* [pp.client-plone](https://pypi.org/project/pp-client-plone): can even mix and match `.` and `-`
* [backport_importlib](https://pypi.org/project/backport_importlib): underscores are pretty rare, but I did find one

However, for `project.version`, this is generally not done today. Almost every package I maintain that follows CalVer eventually gets someone opening an issue because they are mad that the git tags (`2026.01.01` format) don't match the PyPI display (`2026.1.1`). While you can use the zero-padded version in construction the PyPI URL, the display is always the normalized one; this is primarily due to the fact that almost every backend formats it before putting it into the metadata (and PyPI might also load it through `packaging.version.Version`).

Hatchling 1.32.3 finally fixes this. I'm looking at fixing it in other places, but it's hard to fix it when using `packaging.version.Version`, since the original padding gets lost, so you'd have to add `raw_vesrion` or similar everywhere between the metadata and writing out the metadata.

I'd like to propose Version get a `raw_version` attribute. Storing the original string passed to the constructor should be nearly free; it already exists when constructing it, so you are simply bumping the refcount. I think it should be exactly the original string (no stripping whitespace, for example) to avoid any performance regression. I think it could also support being None for versions generated other ways than the standard constructor; an extra None check is a small price for something that's pretty specific in usage. The public accessor could generate a normalized string set to None.

This is not the only way to handle this; we could implement it further down (in pyproject-metadata, for example, or only in the individual backends such as https://github.com/scikit-build/scikit-build-core/pull/1572). Loading and displaying the version should also show the original string, so adding here might help PyPI. It's a pretty specific use case, though. Thoughts?

title: Bug: CLI parses `--include-roles=[]` as `[""]` instead of `[]`
body:
# Bug: CLI parses `--include-roles=[]` as `[""]` instead of `[]`

## Description

When using `pydantic-settings` CLI parsing with a field typed as `list[str]`, passing an empty JSON array works incorrectly.

A non-empty JSON array is parsed correctly:

```bash
--include-roles='["a", "b"]'
```

produces:

```python
include_roles=["a", "b"]
```

However, an empty JSON array:

```bash
--include-roles='[]'
```

produces:

```python
include_roles=[""]
```

instead of:

```python
include_roles=[]
```

## Minimal reproduction

```python
from pydantic import Field
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        cli_parse_args=True,
        cli_kebab_case=True,
        cli_implicit_flags=True,
    )

    include_roles: list[str] = Field(
        default=["person"],
        description='roles decoded by default: comma-separated names (e.g. "person"), or --include-roles=[] for all',
    )


settings = Settings()
print(settings.include_roles)
```

### Working case

```bash
python example.py --include-roles='["a", "b"]'
```

Output:

```text
['a', 'b']
```

### Broken case

```bash
python example.py --include-roles='[]'
```

Output:

```text
['']
```

Expected:

```text
[]
```

## Environment

* Python: `<python version>`
* pydantic: `<pydantic version>`
* pydantic-settings: `<pydantic-settings version>`
* OS: `<OS>`

Configuration:

```python
SettingsConfigDict(
    cli_parse_args=True,
    cli_kebab_case=True,
    cli_implicit_flags=True,
)
```

## Expected behavior

Since `list[str]` supports JSON-style CLI values, an empty JSON array should be parsed in the same way as a non-empty JSON array.

```bash
--include-roles='[]'
```

should result in:

```python
include_roles == []
```

## Actual behavior

The empty array is parsed as a list containing an empty string:

```python
include_roles == [""]
```

## Additional observations

The shell is not the source of the problem. Quoting the argument preserves the JSON string correctly:

```bash
--include-roles='[]'
```

is passed to the application as:

```text
[]
```

Non-empty JSON arrays work correctly:

```bash
--include-roles='["a", "b"]'
```

```python
["a", "b"]
```

The problem appears to be specific to the empty JSON array.

`cli_implicit_flags=True` does not appear to be related to the issue, since it controls implicit boolean CLI flags rather than list parsing.

## Possible cause

The CLI list parsing logic appears to correctly recognize and decode non-empty JSON arrays, but an empty JSON array may subsequently pass through list-item normalization/splitting logic.

Conceptually, the parser appears to turn:

```text
[]
```

into an empty list of values and then normalize the empty value as a list item, resulting in:

```python
[""]
```

rather than preserving:

```python
[]
```

## Suggested regression test

A test similar to the following would catch the issue:

```python
def test_cli_empty_json_list():
    class Settings(BaseSettings):
        model_config = SettingsConfigDict(cli_parse_args=True)

        include_roles: list[str] = ["person"]

    settings = Settings(cli_args=["--include-roles=[]"])

    assert settings.include_roles == []
```

It would also be useful to retain a test for the existing working behavior:

```python
def test_cli_json_list():
    class Settings(BaseSettings):
        model_config = SettingsConfigDict(cli_parse_args=True)

        include_roles: list[str] = ["person"]

    settings = Settings(cli_args=['--include-roles=["a", "b"]'])

    assert settings.include_roles == ["a", "b"]
```

## Impact

This makes it impossible to use the documented JSON list syntax to explicitly specify an empty list from the CLI.

For applications where an empty list has meaningful semantics (for example, "disable filtering" or "include all roles"), this results in a different configuration:

```python
[""]
```

instead of:

```python
[]
```

and can lead to unexpected application behavior.

## Workaround

Currently, the application can work around this by preprocessing the CLI value or by adding a custom validator/parser for this field.

However, this should ideally not be necessary when using JSON syntax for a `list[str]` field.

---

**Expected:** `--include-roles='[]'` → `[]`

**Actual:** `--include-roles='[]'` → `[""]`

title: Is notify_closing after close() allowed? Fix or document
body:
(Despite my suspiciously LLMesque formatting in places, this was all written by a human.)

Currently, [the docs for `notify_closing`](https://trio.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference-lowlevel.html#trio.lowlevel.notify_closing) say:

> So to close something properly, you usually want to do these steps in order:
> 
> 1. Explicitly mark the object as closed, so that any new attempts to use it will abort before they start.
> 2. Call `notify_closing` to wake up any already-existing users.
> 3. Actually close the object.
>
> It’s also possible to do them in a different order if that’s more convenient, *but only if* you make sure not to have any checkpoints in between the steps.

This issue is about that sentence at the end, specifically swapping items 2 and 3: if you close an object before you call `notify_closing`, is that OK (so long as you do both without a checkpoint in between)?

This came up in pull requests #3503 and #3519, which fix #3500; Part of that issue is `notify_closing` failing (even if called in the normal order) in an obscure race condition in guest mode. This issue is more about `notify_closing` (in the wrong order) just in regular non-guest mode usage.

## Very short summary

It turns out that if you close the object before `notify_closing` then that will fail on macOS/BSD (due to a recently-introduced and easily fixable bug), on Windows (due to a much trickier but probably fixable bug) and appear to succeed on Linux but with potentially spurious wait wakes later if the handle had been `dup`ed (and that is impossible to fix).

If you just want to know what to do about that, you can skip to "my suggestions" at the bottom!

## Background: what does notify_closing do?

It isn't obvious why this is needed: ideally, closing a socket would cause the underlying OS wait (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) to wake up any readable/writable wait with some error that indicates that the socket was closed, which we could translate to `ClosedResourceError` at the point we receive it. This doesn't work for reasons that are different on the different IO managers.

**kqueue** When you close a file descriptor, it automatically removes the event subscription from the kqueue. However, the removal is silent: readable/writable waiters aren't notified in any way (there's no "FD was closed" event sent to them), so Trio `wait_readable` / `wait_writable` would wait forever. The `notify_closing` call does two things to fix this:

* Removes the event from the poll set (`_kqueue.control([kevent(fd, filter, KQ_EV_DELETE)], 0)`). As I just said, this happens anyway on close, so this is totally redundant.
* For any waiters (callers of `wait_readable` / `wait_writable`) on that socket, wake immediately with `reschedule(ClosedResourceError)`.

**epoll** Like kqueue, when you close a file descriptor, it removes the event subscription, but this doesn't happen if the socket is `dup`ed (see below). Even if the subscription is removed, waiters aren't notified. `notify_closing` does the same two things:

* Removes event from poll set (`_epoll.unregister(fd)`) - this is not redundant, as the FD could have been `dup`ed.
* Wakes waiters with `reschedule(ClosedResourceError)`.

**IOCP** Unlike the other two, closing the socket actually does notify the waiters (with `AFD_POLL_LOCAL_CLOSE`, which Trio could translate into `ClosedResourceError`, but it currently doesn't). If it were no more complicated than that the IOCP IO manager wouldn't need a `notify_closing` call at all! But Windows has the same issue as epoll that if the socket was `dup`ed then operations continue, so `notify_closing` tidies everything up manually:

* The underlying OS request for waiting is cancelled (`IoCancelEx`)
* Wakes waiters with `reschedule(ClosedResourceError)`.
* Removes the waiters from Trio's little struct that says what to do when the wait operation completes (which it will, later, with a "cancelled" status).


## More background: the issue with dup

If you duplicate the socket handle, like this (taken from a comment in `_io_epoll.py`):

```python
fd1 = open(...)
epoll_ctl(EPOLL_CTL_ADD, fd1, ...)
fd2 = dup(fd1)
close(fd1)
```

Then fd1 is *not* automatically removed from epoll after all. It continues to report events on the old fd1, even though it's closed. Once fd1 is closed, you can't even remove it manually, because it's invalid to call `epoll_ctl` on a closed fd! Even worse, if a new file/socket gets opened on that FD number, then events for the old socket object will continue to appear with no way to distinguish whether they came from the old or new one!

(The comments in the IO manager worry about a busy loop: If a socket is readable/writable but we never remove it from the poll set because we've lost track of it, and because we can't anyway, then `get_events()` would return immediately every time. The epoll code handles this by only issuing one-shot subscriptions so we can't get more than one spurious wake up from an event we've lost track of.)

The same issue occurs on Windows: closing a socket doesn't signal readable/writable waiters if it has been `dup`ed. But it's not as bad because if the event triggers later then it points at the Trio's struct with waiters (which were removed by `notify_closing`) so it can't wake the wrong thing, and it can still be cancelled because cancellation doesn't use the socket handle. (And it can't busy-wait because it's always a one-shot event anyway.)

## What happens if we call close before notify_closing?

Here's what currently happens if you call close then notify_closing, as supposedly permitted by the above text:

* **kqueue** (macOS/BSD): It doesn't work: `wait_readable` / `wait_writable` just continue to wait indefinitely. 
* **IOCP** (Windows): `notify_closing` raises `OSError(10038, 'An operation was attempted on something that is not a socket')`. Regardless of this (i.e. with and without a simple fix for it), `wait_readable` / `wait_writable` do wake, but just as a regular return (not `ClosedResourceError`).
* **epoll** (Linux): Works correctly: `notify_closing` returns normally, and waiters raise `ClosedResourceError`.

However, this all assumes that you haven't called `dup` on the socket. Part of the point of `notify_closing` (in fact the only point of it on Windows) is to handle that case. If you do:

* **kqueue** (macOS/BSD): (Assuming we fix the issue in kqueue `notify_closing` mentioned above) This works fine: kqueue already removed the event based on the file descriptor, regardless of whether it was `dup`ed, so when `notify_closing` attempts to remove it gets an error but ignores it, and then `wait_readable` / `wait_writable` wake and raise `ClosedResourceError`.
* **IOCP** (Windows): (Assuming we fix the issue in IOCP `notify_closing` mentioned above (properly, not using my non-fix suggested below)) Cancellation of the outstanding wait works, and when we get the cancellation notification it points at a struct with no waiters left registered in it.
* **epoll** (Linux): The removal of the pollers doesn't work because the file handle is no longer valid, but waiters do wake and raise `ClosedResourceError`.

## Solving the issue with kqueue `notify_closing` after close

~~This is a recent bug introduced by #3503 to fix #3500 (which fixes a race condition in guest mode which happens even when notify_closing is correctly called before close).~~ If removing the registration from the kqueue fails then, with that change, we bail out from doing anything else. But, if the socket has been closed, then removing from the kqueue has already automatically happened, so it will fail in notify_closing.

I mentioned two fixes in [this comment](https://github.com/python-trio/trio/issues/3500#issuecomment-5587090240) for the `notify_closing` race condition. If we use the other one (if we get an error removing the kqueue registration, continue regardless, but make sure we don't fail later in `process_events` due to a missing `_registered` entry) then that still fixes the race condition and also allows `notify_closing` after close. (When implementing "allowed missing `_registered` entries" as suggested [here](https://github.com/python-trio/trio/pull/3519#discussion_r4057244479), we'll need to include these.) (As a bonus, when this race condition occurs, waiters will get `ClosedResourceError` instead of a plain return.)

## Solving the exception from IOCP `notify_closing` after close

The Windows IOCP IO manager doesn't use regular documented IOCP operations to read and write (because they actually perform the read/write, not just wait for it to be possible synchronously). Instead they use some internal undocumented (but stable) interface called AFD. This requires [translating the socket handle into an internal handle](https://github.com/python-trio/trio/blob/50b9825f7ef6630c2326001cc9323c714c05355d/src/trio/_core/_io_windows.py#L342), which is almost always the same but may not under conditions that happen *just enough* not to ignore.

The first thing `notify_closing()` does is translate the normal handle into the internal one, and uses that to determine which overlapped operation to cancel. If the cancellation fails then that's ignored (which it should be - it could happen due to the same race in #3500). But, first, if the socket is closed then the lookup of the underlying handle fails. This is the cause of the issue in Windows.

I haven't really looked into the best way to solve this yet. It seems that Trio is odd in repeatedly looking up the underlying handle from the socket handle - other frameworks cache this. (Trio does at least cache it for issuing a IOCP cancel due to a Trio task cancellation.) One option for fixing this would be to do that. But I don't really understand why it needs to look up the underlying handle anyway at this point anyway; it's not needed for the cancellation, only to lookup who the waiters are. Why not just key `_afd_waiters` on the user level handle? I guess there's a worry that multiple socket handles could point to the same AFD handle but I don't see how that's possible (but I haven't tried to look into it).

One option suggested by an LLM is, as a fallback, to just assume the underlying handle is the same as the one provided by the caller, which does work in most cases. But I think that's best avoided.

Another option is to just silently return if we can't look up the underlying handle, since `notify_closing` isn't even needed unless the socket was `dup`ed. This would also require turning `AFD_POLL_LOCAL_CLOSE` into  `ClosedResourceError`, which it currently isn't (because currently `notify_closing` cancels the requests anyway). This seems like the best option to me.


## Solving the failed unregistration in epoll after `dup`

For epoll, the big reason to use `notify_closing` is that, after the socket is closed, there's no way to remove waiters from the poll set.

So a version of `notify_closing` that works even if called *after* close is fundamentally impossible. This is a dead end.

The only solution here is to update the documentation to say that this isn't allowed.

I suppose it's worth noting that the consequences are not that catestrophic: the result is just that an unrelated socket might get a spurious wake up for `wait_readable` / `wake_writable`, which will probably be followed by a failed sync call and a retry on the wait.


## Normal return (no exception) from wait readable/writable on a closed socket

While looking into this I noticed a slightly tangential issue.

Regardless of what we notice or fix relating to `notify_closing`, it's always possible for `wait_readable` / `wait_writable` to simply return (rather than raise `ClosedResourceError`) after the socket has been closed, even if following the correct `notify_closing` -> `close` pattern.

That's because this might happen:

1. The IO wait (i.e. `get_events()`) completes, and it includes a regular readable/writable notification.
2. Two tasks are scheduled (in the `runq`): task 1 for some other reason, task 2 because a socket is now readable.
3. The tasks happen to run in this order:
   1. Task 1 resumes and closes the socket (with `notify_closing` then `close`). This does *not* reschedule task 2 because it's no longer waiting from the IO manager's perspective.
   2. Task 2 resumes with a normal return from `wait_readable`.

I notice that the underlying `trio.socket` operations do not handle this. Most of them use `_make_simple_sock_method_wrapper`, which calls `_nonblocking_helper`, which follows a call to `wait_fn` (i.e. `wait_readable` / `wait_writable`) immediately with a call to `fn` (e.g. `socket.recv`). Internally, the Python socket object has set its fd to -1, so this fails with `OSError` (`[Errno 9] EBADF` on Linux, `[WinError 10038] WSAENOTSOCK` on Windows).

It *is* checked by `SocketStream`, which uses [`_translate_socket_errors_to_stream_errors`](https://github.com/python-trio/trio/blob/50b9825f7ef6630c2326001cc9323c714c05355d/src/trio/_highlevel_socket.py#L44) to translate `EBADF` / `ENOTSOCK` to `ClosedResourceError`.

Personally, I'd consider this a bug. If it happened every time, that would be excusable as a design decision, but having a different exception only under a very narrow race seems hard to excuse to me. There are two options for fixing it:

* The wait functions do a last moment check just after `await wait_task_rescheduled()` to see whether the socket has been closed. This would be ideal but they don't have neccesarily access to the `socket` object (the parameter can be a `socket` or a FD int) so they can't necessarily do a quick `fd == -1` check.
* Have the socket operations in Trio `socket` do a check just after the wait function before calling the sync version (or translate errors from the sync call like `SocketStream` does, but not `BrokenResourceError` as that would be a significant breaking change). And add a warning to the documentation of the wait functions that they might fail to raise `ClosedResourceError` for closed files.


## My suggestions

* In the documentation for `notify_closing`:
   * State that it *must* be called before the socket is closed, rather than just "you usually want to".
   * Say that if the socket is closed first then Trio will make a best effort to handle the situation but it's not guaranteed to work.
* kqueue IO manager (macOS/BSD):
  * Use the alternative fix for #3500 `notify_closing` as discussed above (and, in guest mode, add to the set of recently-removed `_registered` entries). I'll do this as part of #3519.
* IOCP IO manager (Windows):
  * When processing events, translate `AFD_POLL_LOCAL_CLOSE` into  `ClosedResourceError`.
  * In `notify_closing`, if there's an error looking up the handle, just return early and hope that socket closure notifies the IOCP (if the socket wasn't `dup`ed) so, with the previous point done, waiters get the correct result.
  * I think these are both fairly low priority since this has been like this for a long time - and we should be recommending against this usage anyway.
* All IO managers:
  * In `wait_readable` and `wait_writable`, if the parameter is not an int then do a last moment check to see if the FD has become -1, and if so then raise `ClosedResourceError`.
* epoll IO manager (Linux):
  * Nothing to do because the `dup` issue is fundamentally unfixable with close before `notify_closing`

title: HeadersDictProxy treats mixed-case duplicate headers as distinct keys
body:
### Describe the bug

`HeadersDictProxy` deduplicates mapping keys with a case-sensitive set. HTTP header names are case-insensitive, and `CIMultiDict` keeps each insertion's original casing, so `X-Foo` and `x-foo` both appear in `list(headers)` / `len(headers)` even though `__getitem__` already joins them.

### To Reproduce

```python
from multidict import CIMultiDict
from aiohttp.helpers import HeadersDictProxy

md = CIMultiDict()
md.add("X-Foo", "1")
md.add("x-foo", "2")
md.add("Host", "a")
headers = HeadersDictProxy(md)

print(list(headers))  # ['X-Foo', 'x-foo', 'Host']
print(len(headers))   # 3
print(list(headers.items()))
# [('X-Foo', '1, 2'), ('x-foo', '1, 2'), ('Host', 'a')]
```

The same split keys show up on parsed request messages:

```python
# GET / HTTP/1.1 + Host: a + X-Foo: 1 + x-foo: 2
# list(msg.headers) == ['Host', 'X-Foo', 'x-foo']
# len(msg.headers) == 3
```

### Expected behavior

One mapping key per case-insensitive header name, keeping the first-seen casing:

```python
list(headers) == ['X-Foo', 'Host']
len(headers) == 2
list(headers.items()) == [('X-Foo', '1, 2'), ('Host', 'a')]
headers["x-foo"] == "1, 2"
```

### Related component

Both (request/response headers exposed via `HeadersDictProxy`)

title: tstring() string portions should not parse :param bind names or \: escapes
body:
The literal string portions of a `tstring()` template are each turned into a `TextClause`, so all of the `text()` parsing rules apply to them: `:name` is taken to be a bound parameter, and `\:` is the escape for a literal colon. None of this is documented or tested for `tstring()`, and it doesn't fit how t-strings work:

```python
from sqlalchemy import tstring, create_engine

x = 5
e = create_engine("sqlite://")
with e.connect() as conn:
    # colon inside a quoted SQL literal is parsed as a bound parameter
    # renders: SELECT ?, 'time is ?'
    # raises: A value is required for bind parameter 'now'
    conn.execute(tstring(t"SELECT {x}, 'time is :now'"))

    # works, but is undocumented; the parameter can't be typed since
    # TString.bindparams() is not supported
    conn.execute(tstring(t"SELECT {x}, :p"), {"p": 10})

    # the escape is an invalid Python escape sequence in a non-raw
    # t-string: SyntaxWarning on Python 3.14
    conn.execute(tstring(t"SELECT {x}, '\:p'"))
```

In a t-string, parameters come from interpolation, so everything outside `{}` should be rendered as-is. The string portions will therefore no longer be scanned for `:name` parameters and will have no escaping rules. The only processing will be what the dialect needs, such as doubling `%` for the `pyformat` and `format` paramstyles. A named parameter can still be used explicitly with `{bindparam("p")}`, or `text()` semantics can be applied to a fragment with `{text(":p")}`.

This is a behavioral change to 2.1.0 / 2.1.1 and is targeted for 2.1.2.

title: How to handle keyword-only arguments
body:
Currently pluggy ignores keyword-only arguments in specs and impls.

The reason historically is that _multicall only called hookimpls using positional arguments (tuple) as an optimization(?), but keyword-only arguments can't be passed positionally.

Since 51ec4486b9d47da944725b0326a412cf9b7518bf however, if a hookimpl function declares a default then we do pass kwargs, so it's possible to support keyword-only.

For specs, supporting keyword-only is less of an issue, since it's not actually called, so it doesn't actually matter.

In pluggy callers are required to pass parameters by keyword so keyword-only or not doesn't make a difference.

Overall, there is no reason to define a keyword-only parameter in either spec or impl, it only has a downside of making calls a bit slower. But I think the current situation where they're just ignored is not very nice. So we can go with either of these:

1. Support them.
2. Reject them (validation).

Since "Support them" is a small performance trap, it seems like 2 is better, unless we can make the performance equivalent, which I will look into.

title: `stream` could send 411 error
body:
While working on #3303 deprecating `get_input_stream`, I noticed that it could be changed to raise `LengthRequired`. I don't think we can actually do this, so I'm writing these notes and closing the issue.

Currently, if the WSGI server does not set `wsgi.input_terminated`, and the client doesn't send `Content-Length`, it's not safe to read from the stream and `get_input_stream` returns an empty `BytesIO`. (It can also return the unsafe stream if `safe_fallback=False` is passed, but `Request.stream` doesn't expose that.)

Instead, it could raise 411 `LengthRequired` to indicate that the client must send a `Content-Length` header. This would also allow code to make its own decision about a fallback, otherwise it's impossible to tell the empty fallback from an empty request without going through all the same checks, `read` returns `b""` for both.

However, this exposes a weird behavior. A request with no body looks the same as an infinite stream up front, neither have `Content-Length`. Therefore, if no body is sent, and the app tried to read the body just in case, it would now return a 411. `Request.form` and `files` currently return empty if there is "no data", which is valid for handling `PUT` with completely optional data, for example. So form parsing needs to catch `LengthRequired`. But then `Request.data` also has the same "problem", etc.

411 seems like a good idea, otherwise the client may have no idea that the application ignored the data it sent, or why. However, it will usually result in some other error anyway, such as form validation failing or not being able to parse an expected body. Given that no one's reported issues with our empty fallback behavior, it doesn't seem like an issue in practice. And it's still possible to detect, with a bit of work, if that's really needed.

title: Deprecate `FileWrapper`
body: It seems to be a less efficient way to iterate over a file rather than just iterating over it directly. It's only yielding 8 kB chunks at a time. The intention of `wsgi.file_wrapper` in WSGI is to expose more efficient file sending from the operating system. The key is optional, our `wrap_file` function is allowed to return the file unchanged if it's not set.

title: PostgreSQL reflection drops columns from composite primary keys when a constraint and a commented object share an OID
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/13614
Originally posted by **Elaskinok** September 28, 2026 ## Describe the bug On PostgreSQL, `_constraint_query`, `_foreing_key_query` and `_check_constraint_query` outer-join `pg_description` on `objoid = pg_constraint.oid` alone. OIDs are only unique within one catalog, so a comment on another object with the same OID as a constraint joins too, and the constraint's rows are repeated once per matching comment. #11961 fixed this for `_comment_query` only. Since 2.0.41 (#10665), `_reflect_constraint` takes the first `indnkeyatts` entries of the aggregated column list as the key and the rest as INCLUDE columns. With repeated rows, composite primary keys and unique constraints lose their trailing columns to `postgresql_include`. Foreign key and check constraints are returned once per matching comment, so the reflected table gets duplicate constraints. ## SQLAlchemy Version in Use 2.0.52 and 2.1.1 ## DBAPI (i.e. the database driver) psycopg2 2.9.12 ## Database Vendor and Major Version PostgreSQL 17 and 18 ## Python Version 3.13 ## Operating system macOS, PostgreSQL in Docker ## To Reproduce ```python import sqlalchemy as sa engine = sa.create_engine("postgresql+psycopg2://scott:tiger@localhost/test") with engine.begin() as conn: conn.exec_driver_sql("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t") conn.exec_driver_sql("CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER, CONSTRAINT t_pkey PRIMARY KEY (a, b))") conn.exec_driver_sql("COMMENT ON CONSTRAINT t_pkey ON t IS 'primary key of t'") # Force an OID collision: a commented large object with the same OID as t_pkey. oid = conn.exec_driver_sql("SELECT oid FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = 't_pkey'").scalar() conn.exec_driver_sql(f"SELECT lo_create({oid})") conn.exec_driver_sql(f"COMMENT ON LARGE OBJECT {oid} IS 'unrelated large object'") print(sa.__version__) print(sa.inspect(engine).get_pk_constraint("t")) print([c.name for c in sa.Table("t", sa.MetaData(), autoload_with=engine).primary_key]) ``` ## Error No exception, but the primary key is wrong (2.1.1 prints the same): ```text 2.0.52 {'constrained_columns': ['a', 'a'], 'name': 't_pkey', 'comment': 'primary key of t', 'dialect_options': {'postgresql_include': ['b', 'b']}} ['a'] ``` Expected `['a', 'b']` for both `constrained_columns` and `Table.primary_key`, with no INCLUDE columns. 2.0.40 also returns duplicates, but its `Table.primary_key` is right: ```text 2.0.40 {'constrained_columns': ['a', 'a', 'b', 'b'], 'name': 't_pkey', 'comment': 'primary key of t'} ['a', 'b'] ``` ## Additional context No large object is needed in practice: `pg_upgrade` keeps table OIDs but gives the recreated constraints new, low OIDs, so a constraint can end up with the OID of a table that has column comments. Code relying on `Table.primary_key` then silently gets a truncated key. I can share a script that reproduces this through `pg_upgrade`. A possible fix is the condition #11961 added to `_comment_query`, applied to the three constraint queries: ```python .outerjoin( pg_catalog.pg_description, sql.and_( pg_catalog.pg_description.c.objoid == pg_catalog.pg_constraint.c.oid, pg_catalog.pg_description.c.classoid == sql.func.cast("pg_catalog.pg_constraint", REGCLASS), ), ) ``` With this applied locally, primary keys, unique constraints, foreign keys and check constraints all reflect correctly under collisions. `_columns_query` is not affected: it also matches `objsubid = attnum`, and only column comments have a nonzero `objsubid`. Alternatively, selecting `pg_catalog.obj_description(pg_constraint.oid, 'pg_constraint')` instead of joining avoids the repeated rows and needs no `REGCLASS` cast, which DuckDB lacks (#12011). The reproduction needs no superuser, so it could double as a test. I can open a PR if that helps.

title: AsyncpgEventBroker: asyncpg sync NOTIFY callback breaks anyio >= 4.14 (NoEventLoopError)
body:
AsyncpgEventBroker: asyncpg sync NOTIFY callback breaks anyio >= 4.14 (`NoEventLoopError`)

### Things to check first

- [x] I have checked that my issue does not already have a solution in the FAQ
- [x] I have searched the existing issues and didn't find my bug already reported there
- [x] I have checked that my bug is still present in the latest release

### Version

4.0.0a6 · anyio 4.14.2 · asyncpg 0.31.0 · Python 3.14

### What happened?

`AsyncScheduler` + `AsyncpgEventBroker` + anyio 4.14.x raises `NoEventLoopError` on **every** `NOTIFY` that arrives (including its own published events on the same connection), so the event is dropped and cross-worker coordination silently breaks.

```
Exception in callback AsyncpgEventBroker._listen_notifications.<locals>.listen_callback()
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../asyncio/events.py", line 94, in _run
    self._context.run(self._callback, *self._args)
  File ".../apscheduler/eventbrokers/asyncpg.py", line 118, in listen_callback
    self._task_group.start_soon(self.publish_local, event)
  File ".../anyio/abc/_tasks.py", line 144, in start_soon
    return self.create_task(call_for_coroutine(func, args), name=final_name)
  File ".../anyio/_backends/_asyncio.py", line 932, in create_task
    return self._spawn(coro, name=name)
  File ".../anyio/_backends/_asyncio.py", line 888, in _spawn
    handle = TaskHandle(coro, name)
  File ".../anyio/_core/_tasks.py", line 259, in __init__
    self._cancel_scope = CancelScope()
  File ".../anyio/_core/_tasks.py", line 60, in __new__
    return get_async_backend().create_cancel_scope(shield=shield, deadline=deadline)
  File ".../anyio/_core/_eventloop.py", line 195, in get_async_backend
    raise NoEventLoopError(...)
anyio.NoEventLoopError: Not currently running on any asynchronous event loop.
```

### Root cause

1. `listen_callback` in `eventbrokers/asyncpg.py:113` is a **plain synchronous** function.
2. asyncpg detects a sync callable and dispatches it via `loop.call_soon()` (`asyncpg/connection.py:1719`), so it runs as a bare callback with **no running asyncio task** (`current_task()` is None).
3. anyio >= 4.14 changed `TaskGroup.start_soon()` to return a `TaskHandle`, and `TaskHandle.__init__` eagerly constructs a `CancelScope()` → `get_async_backend()` → sniffio → raises `NoEventLoopError` because there is no task context. (anyio 4.13 and earlier spawned a plain `asyncio.Task`, which did not hit this path; 4.13 also renamed the private `NoCurrentAsyncBackend` to the public `NoEventLoopError`.)

### How can we reproduce the bug?

Two workers on the same Postgres (or strictly, one worker plus any publisher is enough — the broker also echoes its own `pg_notify` back to its listening connection):

```python
import asyncio
from apscheduler import Scheduler
from apscheduler.datastores.sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemyDataStore
from apscheduler.eventbrokers.asyncpg import AsyncpgEventBroker
from apscheduler.triggers.interval import IntervalTrigger
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

engine = create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@host/db")

async def job():
    print("job ran")

async def main():
    async with Scheduler(
        data_store=SQLAlchemyDataStore(engine),
        event_broker=AsyncpgEventBroker.from_async_sqla_engine(engine),
    ) as scheduler:
        await scheduler.add_job(job, IntervalTrigger(seconds=5), id="job1")
        await scheduler.run_until_stopped()

asyncio.run(main())
```

Expected: events are dispatched to local schedulers via `publish_local`.
Actual: `NoEventLoopError` on every notification; events never dispatched.

A minimal note: pinning anyio to < 4.14 avoids the crash but leaves the sync callback fragile.

### Suggested fix

Make `listen_callback` an `async def`. asyncpg will then wrap it via `loop.create_task()` (`asyncpg/connection.py:1717`), giving it a real task context where `start_soon` works. `remove_listener` takes the same callable, so no other change is needed.

title: AI junk
Harden the release build job GitHub token handling
body:
The release workflow currently checks out the repository with the default persisted GitHub credential and does not explicitly constrain the build job token permissions. The build job only needs repository read access before running `uv build`.

Flask and Werkzeug already use the tighter pattern in their equivalent publish workflows: explicit read-only build permissions and `persist-credentials: false` on checkout.

I have a small patch prepared to apply the same boundary to Jinja without changing release behavior.

title: highlight_words([]) creates zero-length matches
body:
### Description

`Text.highlight_words()` treats an empty word iterable as an empty regular expression. Python's regex engine then finds zero-width matches at every character boundary, so the method reports false matches and appends zero-length spans.

### Steps to reproduce

```python
from rich.text import Text

text = Text("abc")
count = text.highlight_words([], "red")

assert count == 0
assert text._spans == []
```

### Expected behavior

An empty word list should be a no-op and return `0`.

### Actual behavior

The current implementation builds `re_words = ""` and `re.finditer("", "abc")` yields four zero-width matches. `highlight_words()` returns `4` and appends four zero-length spans.

The implementation is in `rich/text.py`, and existing tests only cover non-empty word iterables. I searched existing issues and pull requests for `highlight_words([])` and did not find a matching report.

Would maintainers accept a small guard for an empty word iterable plus a regression test? The repository's contribution guide requires tests and a changelog entry for a bug fix.

title: TypeDecorator.comparator_factory creates a new class with type() on every access
body:
### Describe the bug

`TypeDecorator.comparator_factory` is a property that calls `TypeDecorator._create_td_comparator_type()` on every access, and that function builds a brand new `TDComparator` class with `type()` each time. Nothing is cached, so every new column expression against a `TypeDecorator` type pays for creating a class (about 7.5 us here), and each of those classes can only be freed by the cyclic GC.

This looks like it has been this way since the 2013 `sqlalchemy.sql` refactor. The only thing I found that depends on the closure over `impl` is the pickling support added in fa5682157 (#12002).

### To Reproduce

```python
import timeit

import sqlalchemy
from sqlalchemy import Integer
from sqlalchemy import column
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase
from sqlalchemy.orm import mapped_column
from sqlalchemy.types import TypeDecorator


class Cents(TypeDecorator):
    impl = Integer
    cache_ok = True


class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass


class Item(Base):
    __tablename__ = "item"

    id = mapped_column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    price = mapped_column(Cents)


def best(fn, number):
    return min(timeit.repeat(fn, number=number, repeat=7)) / number * 1e6


cents = Cents()
print(sqlalchemy.__version__, sqlalchemy.__file__)
print(
    "same class on repeated access:",
    cents.comparator_factory is cents.comparator_factory,
)
print(f"cents.comparator_factory     {best(lambda: cents.comparator_factory, 20000):7.2f} us")
print(f"column('x', Cents()) * 2     {best(lambda: column('x', Cents()) * 2, 5000):7.2f} us")
print(f"Item.price * 2               {best(lambda: Item.price * 2, 5000):7.2f} us")
print(f"Item.price == 5              {best(lambda: Item.price == 5, 5000):7.2f} us")
```

### Results

main at 749086adb, CPython 3.14.7, Linux x86_64, no database involved. "pure" means `DISABLE_SQLALCHEMY_CEXT_RUNTIME=1`; I used it for the before/after comparison because my patched checkout has no compiled extensions.

```
                                main (cext)   main (pure)   patched (pure)
same class on repeated access   False         False         True
cents.comparator_factory         7.46 us       7.85 us       0.29 us
column('x', Cents()) * 2        36.68 us      39.08 us      19.72 us
Item.price * 2                  23.80 us      24.58 us      14.85 us
Item.price == 5                  8.30 us       8.48 us       9.01 us   (unchanged, noise)
```

In a larger ORM statement I was profiling (recursive CTE, `with_polymorphic`, window functions, a `TypeDecorator` money column) this was 7 new classes per statement build; building it went from 2.52 ms to 2.43 ms.

### Possible fix

Cache the generated class keyed on `impl.comparator_factory`, since that is the only input `type()` uses. `__reduce__` then pickles that comparator class instead of the impl instance, through a new `_reduce_td_comparator_type()`. The existing `_reduce_td_comparator(impl, expr)` stays, so pickles made by earlier versions still load. The cache can only grow to the number of distinct comparator classes.

I have this on a local branch, with two tests added to `test/sql/test_types.py`: the same class is reused across `TypeDecorator` instances, and the old reduce arguments still unpickle. With the change, `test/sql`, `test/orm`, `test/ext` and `test/base` pass on SQLite (21462 passed, 673 skipped), black and the flake8 setup from the tox `lint` env are clean, and mypy on `lib/sqlalchemy` shows the same 3 greenlet-related errors as unpatched main in my environment.

I can open a PR if this gets `open for pull requests`.

### Environment

- SQLAlchemy: main at 749086adb (2.1.2)
- DBAPI / database: none, no connection is used
- Python: CPython 3.14.7
- OS: Linux x86_64

title: IntervalTrigger uses wall-clock arithmetic across DST on master
body:
### Description

On current master, `IntervalTrigger.next()` adds a timedelta in local wall time. When using `ZoneInfo`, this can produce nonexistent spring-forward times, skip an hour during fall-back, or move backwards when starting in the second fold. The end_time checks also compare wall times when the tzinfo objects are identical.

### Reproduction

```python
from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
from apscheduler.triggers.interval import IntervalTrigger

zone = ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin")
trigger = IntervalTrigger(seconds=1, start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 25, 2, 59, 59, tzinfo=zone))
a = trigger.next()
b = trigger.next()
print(a.isoformat(), b.isoformat())
print(b.timestamp() - a.timestamp())  # 3601.0; expected 1.0
```

A start time in fold=1 can instead move backwards by 3599 seconds. For end_time validation, 02:45 in fold=0 followed by 02:15 in fold=1 is a valid 30-minute interval, but construction raises ValueError.

### Scope and proposed fix

Use UTC datetime arithmetic for elapsed intervals and UTC datetime comparisons for end_time, converting generated times back to the start time's timezone. This preserves microseconds without epoch-float arithmetic.

This concerns the v4 master IntervalTrigger implementation. #1114 fixed the v3 scheduler wakeup calculation; #1137 addresses combining triggers. Neither changes this path.

Verified with Python 3.12 on macOS. Regression tests fail on original source and pass with the fix. OpenAI Codex (GPT-6) assisted with investigation, reproduction, and this report.

title: Plan SpecifierSet mutability, equality, and hash migration
body:
## Problem

`SpecifierSet` is mutable, while `str()`, `hash()`, and equality canonicalize its members. Equal `Specifier` objects can carry different prerelease policies:

```python
s = SpecifierSet([
    Specifier(">=1", prereleases=False),
    Specifier(">=1", prereleases=True),
])
versions = ["1.5a1", "1.5"]
# before str(): True, ['1.5a1', '1.5']
print(str(s))
# after str(): None, ['1.5']
```

`Specifier.__eq__` and `__hash__` intentionally ignore `prereleases`, so changing that contract is not an isolated fix.

## Requested direction

Could this be tracked as a sequenced migration plan rather than an ad hoc canonicalization patch? The plan needs to decide:

- whether to deprecate or restrict `SpecifierSet` mutability first;
- how equality and hash should behave for mutable sets;
- how pickle/state and downstream resolver compatibility are preserved.

Changing equality/hash first could silently alter dependency selection; fixing only canonicalization may imply that hashing is safe while the broader invariant remains unresolved. The previous focused PR was closed after this scope concern was raised; this issue preserves the reproducer without choosing a new rule ad hoc.

title: update docs for `MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH`
body:
Clarify [MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/config/#MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH) should be avoided in the docs in favor of setting the limit on the server just like [its written in the Werkzeug docs](https://werkzeug.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/request_data/#limiting-request-data).

I have this Flask app with Waitress as the production server and MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH set to 10 bytes
```python
from flask import Flask,request
from waitress import serve

app=Flask(__name__)
app.config["MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH"]=10

@app.post("/")
def index():
    print(request.get_data())
    return "OK"

serve(app,listen="localhost:8000")
```
and this client to send data to it until the connection is closed
```python
from urllib.request import urlopen
from random import randbytes

bytes_sent=0
chunk_size=10_000_000
def stream():
    global bytes_sent

    while True:
        yield randbytes(chunk_size)
        bytes_sent+=chunk_size

try:
    urlopen("http://localhost:8000/",stream())
except Exception as e:
    print(e)
print(f"sent around {bytes_sent} bytes")
```
and the app kept receiving and writing the request to disk way over 10 bytes until it hit Waitress's max_request_body_size limit that defaults to 1Gib, with the client printing
```
<urlopen error [WinError 10054] ...>
sent around 1080000000 bytes
```

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13.7
- Flask version: 3.1.3

title: host_is_trusted rejects a bracketed IPv6 address that is in trusted_hosts since 3.1.9
body:
Since 3.1.9, a bracketed IPv6 address in `trusted_hosts` never matches, so a request whose `Host` header is an IPv6 address (for example `[::1]:5017`) is rejected with 400 even though `[::1]` is in the trusted list.

```python
from werkzeug.sansio.utils import host_is_trusted

host_is_trusted("[::1]:5017", ["[::1]"])   # 3.1.8: True   3.1.9: False
host_is_trusted("[::1]", ["[::1]"])        # 3.1.8: True   3.1.9: False
```

Cause: `host_is_trusted` (sansio/utils.py) now takes the hostname from the regex group, so `hostname` is `[::1]`, but each trusted entry is still cut at its first colon (`ref = ref.partition(":")[0]`, line 72), which turns `[::1]` into `[`. Before 3.1.9 both sides were cut the same way, so they happened to compare equal (and any host starting with `[:` matched such an entry, which was its own problem).

A fix could strip a port from a trusted entry only when the entry is not a bracketed IPv6 literal (for example parse it with the same `_host_re` and use its first group).

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13.15
- Werkzeug version: 3.1.9 (3.1.8 behaves as before)

title: Confusing traceback when passing StrEnum instance as Jinja template name
body:
`Environment.get_template` raises a `SyntaxError` when the `name` argument is value whose `__repr__` function is overwritten. In my case, this was caused by an instance of `StrEnum`.

To reproduce, run the following Python code in a directory which contains a `template.jinja` file. The bug is triggered regardless of the template's contents.
```py
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
from enum import StrEnum
env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader("."))

class Templates(StrEnum):
    foo = "template.jinja"

template = env.get_template(Templates.foo)
print(template.render())
```
If `template.jinja` is empty or very short, I get the following traceback:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/USER/dev/jinja/main.py", line 8, in <module>
    template = env.get_template(Templates.foo)
  File "/home/USER/dev/jinja/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/jinja2/environment.py", line 1016, in get_template
    return self._load_template(name, globals)
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/USER/dev/jinja/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/jinja2/environment.py", line 975, in _load_template

    code = environment.compile(source, name, filename)
  File "/home/USER/dev/jinja/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/jinja2/environment.py", line 769, in compile

           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/USER/dev/jinja/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/jinja2/environment.py", line 709, in _compile

  File "template.jinja", line 2
```

If `template.jinja` is a longer file, its 2nd line is shown in the traceback.

title: Deprecate WSGI functions
body:
https://werkzeug.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/levels/#high-or-low suggests that you might want to choose to use the individual utility functions on an `environ` rather than using `Request`. But I'm not sure any of the reasons hold up.

`Request` is an extremely lightweight wrapper around `environ`. There's essentially no cost to constructing it, and then it offers a way better (and more complete) API than the various utility functions. Similarly for `Response`.

Most behavior has already been moved into the sans-io base class, to move towards supporting an ASGI implementation. The utilities that still exist are mostly wrappers around sans-io implementations, but those are all available through the `Request` properties anyway.

Behavior that is truly WSGI-specific (input handling) can either be kept as private helpers, or inlined into the `Request` properties.

This would probably cut down on a lot of #3281 as well, since most of that is for the WSGI utilities.

| utility | `Request` property, etc |
| --- | --- |
| `wsgi.get_current_url` | `url`, `base_url`, `root_url`, `host_url` |
| `wsgi.get_host` | `host` |
| `wsgi.get_content_length` | `content_length` |
| `wsgi.get_input_stream`, `LimitedStream` | `stream` |
| `wsgi.wrap_file`, `FileWrapper` | `send_file`, #3301 |
| `wsgi._RangeWrapper` | already private, `Response.apply_range` #3291 |
| `wsgi.ClosingIterator` | use `Response` as a WSGI application callable |
| `utils.get_content_type` | set `Response.mimetype` |
| `utils.append_slash_redirect` | `Map` `strict_slashes` |
| `formparser.parse_form_data`, `FormDataParser` | `form`, `files` |

title: mssql+pyodbc DATETIMEOFFSET: years before 1000 are formatted without zero padding on Linux, year 1 is stored as 2001
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/13608
Originally posted by **yuansuentw** September 26, 2026 Opening this as a discussion per the bug report guidelines; happy to turn it into an issue if it's confirmed. ### Describe the bug The mssql+pyodbc `DATETIMEOFFSET` bind processor (also used for `DateTime(timezone=True)`) formats values with `strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%f %z")`: https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/rel_2_1_1/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/mssql/pyodbc.py#L493 `%Y` zero-padding is platform dependent, and on Linux (glibc) years before 1000 are not padded. So `datetime(1, 1, 1, tzinfo=utc)` is sent as `'1-01-01 00:00:00.000000 +00:00'`. SQL Server reads the one-digit year using its two-digit-year cutoff and **silently stores 2001-01-01**. Years 100–999 produce `'999-01-01 ...'`, which the server rejects. `0001-01-01 00:00:00 +00:00` is a realistic value: it is .NET's `DateTimeOffset.MinValue`, commonly stored as an "unset" sentinel. Formatting with `value.isoformat(sep=" ")` instead gives `'0001-01-01 00:00:00+00:00'`, which is zero-padded and already has the colon in the offset, so the `re.sub` would no longer be needed. I checked that SQL Server accepts these strings (including year 1, year 999 with microseconds and a `+08:00` offset) via pyodbc `execute` and `executemany`, with `fast_executemany` both on and off, and the stored values are exact. ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use 2.1.1 (the same code is on main) ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver) pyodbc 5.3.0, ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server 18.7.1.1 ### Database Vendor and Major Version SQL Server 2022 (16.0.4210.1) ### Python Version 3.13.2 ### Operating system Linux (Ubuntu 24.04) ### To Reproduce ```python import datetime from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, MetaData, Table, create_engine, insert, select from sqlalchemy.dialects import mssql utc = datetime.timezone.utc # 1. The bind processor output, no database needed d = mssql.pyodbc.dialect() proc = mssql.DATETIMEOFFSET().dialect_impl(d).bind_processor(d) for year in (1, 999, 1000): print(year, repr(proc(datetime.datetime(year, 1, 1, tzinfo=utc)))) # 2. Round trip against SQL Server e = create_engine( "mssql+pyodbc://scott:tiger@localhost:1433/test" "?driver=ODBC+Driver+18+for+SQL+Server&TrustServerCertificate=yes" ) m = MetaData() t = Table("dto_test", m, Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True), Column("v", mssql.DATETIMEOFFSET)) m.drop_all(e) m.create_all(e) with e.begin() as conn: conn.execute(insert(t), {"id": 1, "v": datetime.datetime(1, 1, 1, tzinfo=utc)}) print(conn.scalar(select(t.c.v).where(t.c.id == 1))) # year 2001, expected year 1 with e.begin() as conn: conn.execute(insert(t), {"id": 2, "v": datetime.datetime(999, 1, 1, tzinfo=utc)}) # raises ``` ### Error ``` 1 '1-01-01 00:00:00.000000 +00:00' 999 '999-01-01 00:00:00.000000 +00:00' 1000 '1000-01-01 00:00:00.000000 +00:00' 2001-01-01 00:00:00+00:00 Traceback (most recent call last): File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/base.py", line 1943, in _exec_single_context self.dialect.do_execute( ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^ cursor, str_statement, effective_parameters, context ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ) ^ File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/default.py", line 1180, in do_execute cursor.execute(statement, parameters) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ pyodbc.DataError: ('22007', '[22007] [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server][SQL Server]Conversion failed when converting date and/or time from character string. (241) (SQLExecDirectW)') The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception: Traceback (most recent call last): File "test.py", line 29, in conn.execute(insert(t), {"id": 2, "v": datetime.datetime(999, 1, 1, tzinfo=utc)}) # raises ~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/base.py", line 1448, in execute return meth( self, distilled_parameters, execution_options or NO_OPTIONS, ) File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/sql/elements.py", line 533, in _execute_on_connection return connection._execute_clauseelement( ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^ self, distilled_params, execution_options ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ) ^ File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/base.py", line 1668, in _execute_clauseelement ret = self._execute_context( dialect, ...<9 lines>... param_dict=param_dict, ) File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/base.py", line 1822, in _execute_context return self._exec_single_context( ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^ dialect, context, statement, parameters ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ) ^ File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/base.py", line 1962, in _exec_single_context self._handle_dbapi_exception( ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^ e, str_statement, effective_parameters, cursor, context ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ) ^ File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/base.py", line 2332, in _handle_dbapi_exception raise sqlalchemy_exception.with_traceback(exc_info[2]) from e File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/base.py", line 1943, in _exec_single_context self.dialect.do_execute( ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^ cursor, str_statement, effective_parameters, context ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ) ^ File ".../site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/default.py", line 1180, in do_execute cursor.execute(statement, parameters) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ sqlalchemy.exc.DataError: (pyodbc.DataError) ('22007', '[22007] [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server][SQL Server]Conversion failed when converting date and/or time from character string. title: genesis edge
Connection pool can close a connection it has already assigned to a queued request
body:
`_assign_requests_to_connections` assigns an idle connection to a queued request, but the connection stays `IDLE` until the waiting thread wakes up and calls `handle_request`. In between, another thread's pass still sees it as idle and closes it (surplus keep-alive, or "close an idle connection to make room" at `max_connections`). `HTTP11Connection.close` doesn't check the state.

If the request hasn't started yet, `handle_request` raises `ConnectionNotAvailable` and the request is re-queued. If it has, the socket is closed under a request waiting for its response. On Linux the blocked `poll()` isn't woken by the close, so the request hangs until its read timeout.

Seen with the sync pool through httpx and the openai client, 342 threads, `max_connections=100`, `max_keepalive_connections=20`: 2 to 3 requests per run hang for the full read timeout. Instrumenting the pool shows the closed connection was referenced by a `PoolRequest` in `_requests` when the pass decided to close it, and `close` running on an `ACTIVE` connection at the time of each timeout.

httpcore 1.0.9 and master (10a6582). Fix in #1111.

title: test_connect_to_selfsigned_fails can time out before certificate verification
body:
### Describe the bug

Hej,

I found this while reviewing the CI failures for #14681.

The Windows job intermittently failed in `tests/test_builders/test_build_linkcheck.py::test_connect_to_selfsigned_fails` because the HTTPS request reached its 0.25-second read timeout before certificate verification completed.

The test expects the self-signed certificate to produce:

```text
status: broken
info:   ... [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] ...
```

Instead, linkcheck can report:

```text
status: timeout
info:   ... Read timed out. (read timeout=0.25)
```

This is a test-infrastructure timing failure.

### How to Reproduce

The failure is intermittent. On Windows, repeatedly run:

```powershell
1..200 | ForEach-Object {
    Write-Host "Attempt $_"
    uv run pytest -q `
        tests/test_builders/test_build_linkcheck.py::test_connect_to_selfsigned_fails

    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
        exit $LASTEXITCODE
    }
}
```

It may be easier to reproduce under the load and scheduling of the complete test suite:

```powershell
uv run pytest -vv --durations 25
```

An example occurred in this Windows CI job: https://github.com/sphinx-doc/sphinx/actions/runs/35436525563/job/105880014681

### Environment Information

```text
Platform: Windows
Python version: 3.14.7
Sphinx version: 9.1.1+/d85f0ae
Docutils version: 0.22.4
pytest version: 9.1.1
```

### Sphinx extensions

```python
[]
```

### Additional context

The same test and failure mode were previously reported in #12038.
That issue was closed after increasing the linkcheck test timeout and adding a server readiness check.
Those changes reduced the frequency of the failure but did not eliminate it.
